newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's "Death Capital" relaxed place to die.
newsitem.headline: Australia's "Death Capital" relaxed place to die.

text.p: This sleepy coastal city in the country's far north, with its laid-back attitude and sunny tropical days, is an unlikely setting for Australia's "Death Capital".

But critics of the Northern Territory's controversial voluntary euthanasia law, the world's first measure legalising mercy killings, fear this small capital will soon become the centre of a death industry as dying people flock to use the law.

The death last week of popular local Bob Dent, the first person to take his own life under the law, has renewed debate among the fiercely independent residents of the territory, who resent interference from "down south".
Public opinion on the streets of Darwin, where most of the 70,000 residents dress casually for the hot weather, is overwhelmingly in favour of the territory's mercy killing law.
"People are suffering for five or six years before they finally croak it," council worker Jack Jones told Reuters.
"If they are mentally capable enough...then they should be able to do it."

Several terminally-ill people had already travelled thousands of kilometres to this isolated city hoping to die under the territory law, leading euthanasia campaigner doctor Philip Nitschke told Reuters.
Darwin mayor George Brown rejects the idea that the mercy killing law will sully his city's reputation.
"I don't think this will hurt our image," he told Reuters.
"I think more and more that people are realising that we're not a frontier, we are just as sophisticated as any other Australian city."
Nitschke, too, dismisses the "Death Capital" tag, although he concedes it may well be so in the short-term.
"But eventually, as other states see how successfully it (the law) operates, they'll come under pressure from their own constituencies to pass similar legislation," he said.
An anonymous letter writer to the local newspaper, the Northern Territory News, attacked critics of the law.
"These are heartless, callous, ignorant people who wish to see our grandmothers and grandfathers suffering without relief," said the writer, who signed the letter "the Lone Rainger".
But support is not unanimous.
"We should be ashamed of such a law," mother-of-three Therese de Souza said.

Darwin, Australia's smallest capital city, is closer to Asia than Sydney. It's also the country's most Asian city, with substantial Indonesian, Thai, Filipino and Timorese communities and Asian-style street markets.
Territory authorities have declared this city Australia's gateway to Asia, and shiploads of exports such as live cattle constantly leave for the booming economies to the north.
The terriroty's residents, many of whom have moved here from elsewhere in Australia, are famous for their hospitality and their rough-and-tumble casualness.
Perhaps ironically for a city where the mostly-elderly, terminally-ill come to die, Darwin is a young city, with an average age well under 30 and several years below the rest of the country.

Many people are here with the military as part of Australia's defence concentration along the north, or work in sectors supporting the territory's giant mining and live cattle industries and growing tourism sector.
